clue.text: Vehicle fit only for the breakers

definitions.text: Vehicle fit only for the breakers

parts.words: Vehicle fit only for the breakers
parts.note: breakers sound like vandals who would wreck a car, but they are waves, and the vehicle is a plank ridden on them

explanation.surface: A car so battered that only the scrapyard wreckers would want it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breakers' suggests a breaker's yard for scrapped cars; here they are breaking waves, and the only vehicle fit for them is the board a surfer rides.
explanation.definitionFit: A surfer's plank carries its rider over waves, so it is a vehicle used only among breakers.

clue.text: Wear when defrocking?

parts.note: defrocking a priest is dismissing (sacking) a member of the cloth, and the coarse garment of penitence fits that picture

explanation.surface: What to put on at the ceremony when a priest is thrown out of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: Defrocking a clergyman is literally sacking the cloth; the garment of mourning and penance is made of exactly those two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse penitential fabric was worn as a sign of mourning or remorse, so it is something to wear.

clue.text: They're known by experience

parts.note: an experienced person is said to know the cords of the trade, from sailors learning a ship's rigging

explanation.surface: Things one only learns by having been through them.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'to know the ropes' means to be experienced in how something works; a sailor learned a ship's rigging only by working it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says a veteran knows the cords of the rigging, meaning the practical procedures learnt over time.

clue.text: Glass, reflecting public opinion perhaps

definitions.meaning: a weather glass is the household instrument that shows atmospheric pressure
a gauge of public feeling, as in a poll taken as an indicator of the national mood

explanation.surface: A mirror that shows what the public thinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glass' suggests a mirror, which 'reflecting' supports; in fact it is the old word for the instrument hanging in the hall that measures air pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: A weather glass measures air pressure, and figuratively any indicator of the public mood, such as a poll, is called by the same name.

clue.text: There is a willow grows — a brook " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: There is a willow grows — a brook " (Hamlet)

parts.words: There is a willow grows — a brook " (Hamlet)
parts.note: the missing word completes Gertrude's line in Hamlet describing the tree leaning over the stream where Ophelia drowned

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Hamlet with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Gertrude's speech on Ophelia's death opens 'There is a willow grows aslant a brook'; the solver fills the gap with the word for leaning across at an angle.
explanation.definitionFit: The willow leans across the stream at a slant, which is the meaning of the missing adverb.

clue.text: You must make up your mind to make it

definitions.text: You must make up your mind to make it

parts.words: You must make up your mind to make it
parts.note: a resolution is something reached only by settling one's thoughts, so 'make it' refers to making a choice

explanation.surface: Advice that success requires firm resolve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make it' sounds like succeeding, but 'it' is the thing made: you make a choice by making up your mind.
explanation.definitionFit: A choice or resolution is precisely what one makes by making up one's mind.

clue.text: Present-day receipts

parts.note: read as 'present day', meaning a birthday or Christmas, these are the things received then

explanation.surface: Modern-day bills of sale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present-day' looks like 'modern', and 'receipts' like slips of paper; read instead as a day of presents, the receipts are the things received.
explanation.definitionFit: On a birthday or at Christmas the things received are presents, so they are that day's receipts.

clue.text: Not the best man in stable employment

definitions.text: Not the best man in stable employment

parts.words: Not the best man in stable employment
parts.note: at a wedding the man who is not the best man is the ..., and the same word means a stable hand who looks after horses

explanation.surface: A man of middling ability holding down a secure job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable employment' suggests a secure job; it is literal work in a stable. At a wedding the bridegroom is the man beside the best man.
explanation.definitionFit: A stable lad who tends horses shares his title with the bridegroom, the wedding's central man who is not the best man.

clue.text: Made a 28 discovery — on one's doorstep?

parts.note: to found something is to make or establish it
28 across is fishy, so 'a 28' is a fishy thing, here the ling, a fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Someone discovered something suspicious lying on their front step.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points to 28 across, so 'a 28' stands for a fish. An abandoned baby left on a doorstep is the classic picture behind the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant abandoned by its parents and found by strangers, often left on a doorstep, is a discovery of this kind.

clue.text: Is set in different locations

indicators.note: the letters of 'Is set' are put in a different order, which signals rearrangement

explanation.surface: Something is placed in various spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges IS SET; 'in' only links fodder to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Places where something is or will be located are its locations.

clue.text: Top examination of tobacco

parts.note: a cap is a top, as on a bottle or pen
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A leading inspection of tobacco products.
explanation.walkthrough: Caporal is a French-style dark tobacco, the 'tabac caporal' once common in cigarettes.
explanation.definitionFit: Caporal is a strong French variety of the leaf, smoked in cigarettes and pipes.

clue.text: Dodgsonian game, including flamingoes and hedgehogs

definitions.text: Dodgsonian game, including flamingoes and hedgehogs

parts.words: Dodgsonian game, including flamingoes and hedgehogs
parts.note: Charles Dodgson wrote as Lewis Carroll, and in Alice in Wonderland the Queen's lawn game uses flamingoes as mallets and hedgehogs as balls

explanation.surface: A description of the strange lawn game in Alice in Wonderland.
explanation.walkthrough: Dodgson is Lewis Carroll's real name; at the Queen of Hearts' party Alice plays the hoop-and-mallet lawn game with live animals.
explanation.definitionFit: The lawn game with mallets, balls and hoops is played in Wonderland with flamingoes and hedgehogs.

clue.text: Keats's nightingale charmed magic ones

parts.note: in Ode to a Nightingale, Keats's bird's song 'Charm'd magic' windows opening on perilous seas

explanation.surface: A line about the enchanting effect of the bird in Keats's ode.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's Ode to a Nightingale has 'Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam / Of perilous seas'; 'ones' stands for the missing noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote of hinged windows opening on the foam, so the plural noun for such windows completes his phrase.

clue.text: Sovereign that made what sovereigns were made of

definitions.text: Sovereign that made what sovereigns were made of

parts.words: Sovereign that made what sovereigns were made of
parts.note: the first sovereign is a king of Greek legend, the second the British gold coin; the king turned all he touched to gold

explanation.surface: A monarch who minted coins.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is also an old British gold coin. The legendary Phrygian king had the golden touch, so he made gold, the coins' metal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phrygian king of legend was a ruler, and his touch turned things to gold, the coin's metal.

clue.text: A tenor in extravagant make-up

indicators.note: the letters of 'A tenor' are made up into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A singer wearing flamboyant stage make-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make-up' looks like greasepaint but signals that the letters of A TENOR are rearranged; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaborately decorated and showy work is extravagant in style.

clue.text: Limit of feline endurance

parts.note: by proverb a cat survives many deaths, and the number of its allotted lives is the limit

explanation.surface: How much a cat can put up with.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb gives a cat that many lives, so they mark how far its survival can stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Folklore grants a cat a fixed number of lives, the most deaths it can survive.

clue.text: The dying swan is one

parts.note: legend says the swan sings once, as it dies, its swan song, which would make it a singing bird

explanation.surface: A reference to the famous ballet role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Dying Swan' suggests the ballet solo; the legend of the swan song, sung only at death, makes the dying swan a singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend has the swan sing beautifully only as it dies, so in death it is a singing bird.

clue.text: He threw his arms about in deadly fashion

definitions.text: He threw his arms about in deadly fashion

parts.words: He threw his arms about in deadly fashion
parts.note: 'arms' sounds like limbs flailing, but they are hand bombs, and the soldier threw them

explanation.surface: A man flailing his limbs wildly and dangerously.
explanation.walkthrough: The soldier was originally named for throwing grenades, so the 'arms' he threw were weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: The original soldiers of this kind were trained to throw hand bombs, deadly arms thrown about.

clue.text: An old star wandering in Staffordshire

definitions.note: a place name defined by its location, a noun phrase for a town

indicators.note: the letters of 'An old star' wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A former celebrity wandering around the English Midlands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering' rearranges AN OLD STAR. Darlaston is a town in the Black Country, historically in Staffordshire, an English Midlands county.
explanation.definitionFit: Darlaston is a Black Country town that lay in the Midlands county, so it is a place there.

clue.text: Like Satan without his attendant imps

definitions.text: Like Satan without his attendant imps

parts.words: Like Satan without his attendant imps
parts.note: a mischievous imp is called a limb of the devil, so Satan without imps has lost his limbs

explanation.surface: The devil left alone without his little helpers.
explanation.walkthrough: A naughty child or imp is called 'a limb of Satan'; take away the imps and the devil is without his limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is called a limb of Satan, so a devil without imps has lost his arms and legs.

clue.text: By the way, it's something to grasp

definitions.text: By the way, it's something to grasp

parts.words: By the way, it's something to grasp
parts.note: 'by the way' sounds like an aside, but read literally it means beside a path or stair, where a bar is held

explanation.surface: An offhand remark that there is an idea worth understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By the way' sounds like 'incidentally', and 'grasp' like understanding; literally, beside the way up a staircase is the bar you grip.
explanation.definitionFit: The bar running beside a staircase or walkway is there to be held for support.

clue.text: Just the book to keep on the the shelf

definitions.text: Just the book to keep on the the shelf

parts.words: Just the book to keep on the the shelf
parts.note: a shelf is a ledge, and the book of accounts has that word inside its name

explanation.surface: A recommendation of the right volume for a bookcase.
explanation.walkthrough: The paper prints 'the the', a typesetting slip. An account book's name begins with the word for a shelf, so it is the book to keep on a ledge.
explanation.definitionFit: An account book is a book kept by a bookkeeper, and its name opens with the word for a narrow shelf.

clue.text: Snooker, 'of course'

parts.note: to snooker is to block a shot, and on a golf course the old term for one ball blocking another's line to the hole means the same

explanation.surface: Naturally, the game is snooker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' sounds like 'naturally', but it is the golf course: on the green, a ball blocking the path to the hole was a snooker of the golfing kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean to obstruct a shot; the golfing term names one ball blocking another's line to the hole.

clue.text: Divide the port

definitions.meaning: to divide is to separate into parts
a harbour city on Croatia's Dalmatian coast

explanation.surface: An instruction to share out the fortified wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The port' looks like the after-dinner wine; it is a harbour city in Croatia.
explanation.definitionFit: To separate into parts is a verb sense; the Adriatic harbour city in Croatia shares the spelling.

clue.text: They run the show, to keep the flag flying?

definitions.meaning: the people employed to run an organisation
a pole holding a flag aloft, as in flagstaff

explanation.surface: The organisers of an event keep patriotic spirits up.
explanation.walkthrough: A flag flies from a pole, the flagstaff, so the second sense is that pole.
explanation.definitionFit: The employees who run an organisation are its workforce, and the pole holding a flag aloft is a flagpole of that name.

clue.text: Wait — with black looks ?

definitions.meaning: to linger or stay for a while

explanation.surface: Someone hanging about, glowering darkly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black looks' suggests scowls; literally it is something that looks black, coated with tar.
explanation.definitionFit: To linger is to delay, and something coated in pitch looks black.

clue.text: Mr. Toad's family

parts.note: Mr Toad of The Wind in the Willows sounds like a household, but the family here is the zoological order of frogs and toads

explanation.surface: The relatives of Toad of Toad Hall from The Wind in the Willows.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Toad is the hero of Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows; his 'family' is the biological group of tailless amphibians.
explanation.definitionFit: The zoological order of tailless amphibians includes all toads, so it is any toad's family in the biological sense.

clue.text: Such a remarkable place to house women!

definitions.text: Such a remarkable place to house women!

indicators.note: the phrase 'Such a remarkable' houses the answer inside its letters, spanning the words

explanation.surface: An exclamation at an extraordinary home for women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' signals the hidden word: it runs through 'sucH A REMarkable'. The whole clue also defines the quarters for wives in a Muslim household.
explanation.definitionFit: The secluded quarters for wives and concubines in a Muslim household are a place set aside for women.

clue.text: Not in favour of giving publicity to poetry

parts.note: an ad is a piece of publicity
verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Someone opposed to promoting poems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'giving' and 'to' join the pieces; the definition is the whole opening phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposed to or hostile towards something is to be against it, not in favour.

clue.text: I'm great as a police inspector

indicators.note: the letters of 'I'm great' are turned into another word, as a new form, signalling rearrangement

explanation.surface: A detective boasting of his own brilliance.
explanation.walkthrough: Maigret is Georges Simenon's fictional detective of the Paris police; the letters of I'M GREAT rearrange to his name.
explanation.definitionFit: Georges Simenon's fictional Paris detective holds the rank of commissaire, an officer of the police.

clue.text: Suspicious if backward and retiring

indicators.note: the word 'if' is read backward, turning it round

parts.note: retiring means shy, modest

explanation.surface: Someone shy and backward seems suspicious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' reverses IF to FI; 'and' links it to SHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dubious that arouses suspicion is described as smelling bad, like stale fish.

clue.text: Guide to the Cattle Market?

parts.note: a guide sounds like a handbook, but a man at a cattle market sells bullocks, and the person who guides a ship has a name that splits that way

explanation.surface: The title of a handbook for farmers buying livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: A guide here is the person at the helm; split differently his title reads as a man of bullocks, fitting a cattle market.
explanation.definitionFit: The person at the helm guides a ship, and his title splits into young bullocks plus a man.
